drills.title: Defensive line · Whistle then advance together
drills.objective: Build the simplest defensive-line reaction: on a coach's whistle all six U10 defenders move two short steps forward together, preserve their spacing, then hold their shape. Use this before the carry-or-pass decision drill.
drills.safety: Non-contact reaction drill. Keep a clear run-off and stop the line well before the coach or attacker. The whistle is a coach's practice cue, not a substitute for checking current RFU U10 offside and restart requirements. Never treat this as permission to rush a free pass from an illegal starting position.

frames.name: Set up · six defenders connected
frames.notes: Six defenders form a line at even spacing. The coach stays in the same position as in the later carry-or-pass drill. Explain: react to the whistle together, then stop square and balanced. The attacker and ground ball stay still.

frames.name: Whistle · advance two short steps together
frames.notes: The coach blows the whistle. All six defenders step forward immediately and in unison, without sprinting into contact. Eyes up, spacing unchanged. They must be legally onside before moving in a real restart.

frames.name: Hold shape · look and communicate
frames.notes: Pause and check that the line is still connected, everyone is facing the play and nobody has sprinted out alone. Repeat several times before adding a ball-carrier decision.

drills.players: Six defenders (D1–D6), one support attacker (A1), one coach/ball feeder. Start with all six defenders across the same line. The coach and A1 are behind them, with A1 slightly deeper to receive.
drills.equipment: One rugby ball and four cones to mark an 11 × 20 m working area. No contact pads are required for the touch version.
drills.instructions: 1. Set out the six-defender line as shown. Coach and supporting runner remain in their starting positions. 2. Explain that this is a whistle-reaction exercise, not permission to cross an offside line. 3. Blow the whistle and ask every defender to advance two short steps together. 4. Stop, check spacing and communication, reset, then repeat. 5. Progress to Hold the line · Carry or pass? after the group can move together.
drills.coaching: Coach the timing of the FIRST step, not an all-out sprint. Keep shoulders square, communication short and the line connected. Use the pause to ask who moved early or late. Keep all actions non-contact. At a real U10 free pass, ensure the defenders have retired the required distance and only advance when lawfully permitted.
drills.regression: Start with slower calls and two small steps. Stop if any defender sprints ahead or loses spacing.
drills.progression: Next: Hold the line · Carry or pass? (seed-133). The same defensive line and coach position now develop into two decision outcomes.
drills.questions: Did all six move on the whistle together? Was there a gap after the first step? Can you say which teammate you must stay connected with?
drills.notes: This drill contains two real playable outcomes after a shared whistle and defensive advance. Playback stops at the diamond. Choose A or B and the animation continues with different ball possession and defender reactions. The standard video export plays A and B in labelled chapters; the coaching sheet shows both. The illustrations are coach-authored examples, not automatic tactical predictions or official RFU material.

drills.title: Hold the line · Carry or pass?
drills.objective: Defenders move together, scan for the ball carrier and close the right channel without losing the line. The attack has a genuine choice: the coach carries, or passes backwards to A1.
drills.safety: U10 activity: begin with touch for both outcomes. Never ask children to tackle an adult coach. The adult-carry outcome is always a two-hand touch demonstration. If practising the A1 tackle, use only age-matched participants with an appropriately qualified coach, a progressive tackle warm-up, controlled speed and the current RFU tackle-height requirement. Head to the safe side, stable feet, shoulder-and-arm connection, and a complete wrap—not a head-first or diving contact. D5 is a covering defender, not a second simultaneous tackler. Stop immediately if spacing or head position becomes unsafe; the player who goes to ground must release and present safely. Confirm current RFU Regulation 15 Appendix 4 before the session.

frames.name: Set up · six defenders and two attackers
frames.notes: Six defenders start connected across the pitch. Coach and A1 stand behind the ball. The four cones mark a working area; A1 begins deeper so the eventual pass can travel backwards.

frames.name: Coach collects the ball
frames.notes: Coach picks up the grounded ball. Defenders stay ready and communicate their spacing; A1 waits deeper for a possible pass.

frames.name: WHISTLE · GO — read the carrier
frames.notes: The whistle starts the movement. Coach runs towards the defensive line, while all six defenders take small steps up together. At the yellow diamond, STOP and choose A or B.

decision.question: Open gap?
decision.cue: Look on defense movement to spot possible gaps.

options.label: Coach carries · D1 and D2 close for touch
Coach passes · A1 attacks D4's channel

frames.name: B1 · Backwards pass to A1
frames.notes: Coach passes backwards across to A1, who stays deeper until the ball arrives. D4 calls the receiver; D5 covers the neighbouring channel while the remaining defenders stay connected.

frames.name: B2 · A1 attacks; D4 tackles
frames.notes: A1 receives, looks up and carries into the outside channel. D4 tracks A1, shortens steps and makes the controlled tackle using safe head placement and a wrap. D5 closes the adjacent gap as cover; D5 does not join the tackle.

frames.name: B3 · Release and present
frames.notes: D4 releases and gets back to feet. A1 goes to ground safely, releases and presents the ball away from pressure. D5 stays on feet and does not dive into the contact area. Reset the players and repeat with the other outcome.

drills.players: Six defenders (D1–D6), one support attacker (A1), one coach/ball feeder. Start with all six defenders across the same line. The coach and A1 are behind them, with A1 slightly deeper to receive.
drills.equipment: One rugby ball and four cones to mark an 11 × 20 m working area. No contact pads are required for the touch version.
drills.instructions:
Set up D1–D6 in a connected defensive line. The ball begins on the ground by the coach; A1 waits deeper and to the opposite side. On the whistle, defenders take a few controlled steps forward together. The coach runs towards the line and a decision is reached. PAUSE: choose A or B.
A — Carry: the coach keeps the ball and runs into the near-side channel. D1 and D2 close the space and make a two-hand TOUCH on the adult coach. Stop and reset.
B — Pass: the coach passes backwards to A1. D4 tracks A1 into the outside channel and completes a controlled tackle; D5 closes the space as cover, not as a simultaneous second tackler. A1 releases and presents the ball. Reset to the same start after either option.
Try both outcomes. For the players, avoid announcing which option the coach will choose until the defenders have started moving.
drills.coaching:
DEFENCE — Go together on GO, not six separate sprints. Look across the line and talk: 'UP', 'BALL', 'MY SIDE'. Shorten steps as the carrier approaches. The closest player tracks the hips; the next defender covers the space beside them. Everyone else stays connected and watches for the pass.
ATTACK — Pick up securely, eyes up and choose space. When passing, keep A1 behind the carrier and send the ball backwards. A1 catches before accelerating; keep the ball available after a legal tackle.
Keep the tempo modest. One good read and one good call are more valuable than a big collision.
drills.regression: First walk it through with defenders knowing the option. Use two-hand touch on every carrier, keep the pass simple and allow a verbal pause so the defenders can identify their responsibilities.
drills.progression: Do not reveal A or B until the coach reaches the decision. Vary the channel, move the receiving attacker to a new starting position (still behind for the pass), or shorten the time defenders have to communicate. Increase pace only after the defensive line stays organised; contact is a separate technical progression.
drills.questions: Who noticed the ball changing hands first? Did all six defenders move up together? Which two players were responsible for the channel, and who kept the line connected? Was the pass backwards? Could you stop the run with safe positioning rather than a rushed hit?
drills.notes: This drill contains two real playable outcomes after a shared whistle and defensive advance. Playback stops at the diamond. Choose A or B and the animation continues with different ball possession and defender reactions. The standard video export plays A and B in labelled chapters; the coaching sheet shows both. The illustrations are coach-authored examples, not automatic tactical predictions or official RFU material.

branching.question: Ball carrier's choice: carry into the gap or pass to A1?

choices.label: Coach carries · D1 and D2 close for touch

frames.name: A1 · Carry into the near-side channel
frames.notes: Coach keeps the ball and accelerates through the near-side gap. D1 calls the carrier, D2 covers the inside, and the other defenders remain connected. D1 and D2 stop the adult coach with two-hand touch only.

frames.name: A2 · Two-hand touch · stop and reset
frames.notes: Freeze when D1 and D2 have closed the channel. Count the touch; do not make a live tackle on the adult. Ask who called the ball and whether the rest of the line stayed connected.

choices.explanation: The coach keeps the ball and carries into the inside channel. The nearest two defenders close the gap and finish with two-hand touch. Children must not tackle an adult coach.
choices.watchFor: D2 and D3 communicate, close space without diving in and hold the inside. The other defenders keep their channels rather than chasing the coach.

choices.label: Coach passes · A1 attacks D4's channel

frames.name: B1 · Backwards pass to A1
frames.notes: Coach passes backwards across to A1, who stays deeper until the ball arrives. D4 calls the receiver; D5 covers the neighbouring channel while the remaining defenders stay connected.

frames.name: B2 · A1 attacks; D4 tackles
frames.notes: A1 receives, looks up and carries into the outside channel. D4 tracks A1, shortens steps and makes the controlled tackle using safe head placement and a wrap. D5 closes the adjacent gap as cover; D5 does not join the tackle.

frames.name: B3 · Release and present
frames.notes: D4 releases and gets back to feet. A1 goes to ground safely, releases and presents the ball away from pressure. D5 stays on feet and does not dive into the contact area. Reset the players and repeat with the other outcome.

choices.explanation: The coach passes backwards to A1. The outside defenders track the new ball carrier, with one controlled age-matched tackler and a covering defender in the demonstration.
choices.watchFor: Watch the backward pass, D4's approach to the ball carrier and D5's covering position. The tackle must be controlled and supervised by a qualified coach.

branching.context: The first movement is the same in both cases: the defensive line advances together on the whistle. The choice comes when the ball is played. Defenders must identify the actual carrier before changing their shape.
branching.watchFor: Look at the first two steps: are all six defenders moving on the same cue, with their spacing intact? Then watch which defenders communicate and adjust to the carrier.

drills.title: Defender clear-out over bag
drills.objective: After losing possession at recent tackles, we want players to stop watching and get involved. The first support player arrives promptly, makes a safe, strong position over the contact area and protects possession. The next support player is already ready to move the ball away. Success is quick support followed by a useful pass, not simply winning a pushing contest.
drills.safety: Controlled contact practice only, not a full match ruck: the rugby ball is deliberately to the side of the sausage bag. D1 must be able to hold the shield securely and remain balanced; A1 begins at walking pace against gentle resistance. Stop any charging, head-down entry, contact near the head/neck, collapsing, twisting, lifting, falling onto the bag or stepping on another player. Both players stay on their feet with heads and shoulders above hips. Keep A2 and D2 out of the physical contest and avoid collisions with waiting players. Check the bag cannot roll or trip anyone and keep the nearby ball outside the players' feet. In actual U10 play, ruck participation is limited to two from each side; players must join from their own side and the ball must be used promptly after 'Use it!' (five seconds). Only progress to opposed contact under a suitably experienced, RFU-aligned club coach after a practical risk check.

frames.name: Set up and explain
frames.notes: Four attackers and four defenders are queued on opposite sides. D1 carries the shield; the sausage bag lies on the grass and the separate rugby ball is to its side. A1 will be first support and A2 will play the ball. Coach explains why arriving promptly matters. This is a technique station; check which direction would be onside in a real match.

frames.name: Arrive and make contact
frames.notes: A1 moves to the bag as D1 brings in the shield. Their contact is controlled and on their feet; A1 works against the pad, not D1's head or neck. A2 and D2 move into waiting positions without joining. Watch the posture and approach before introducing any push.

frames.name: Controlled contest
frames.notes: A1 and D1 make a short, low-force push–pull over the grounded bag. In this demonstration A1 secures the space and D1 yields. A2 moves to the separate ball late in the step, but may only touch it when the coach calls 'Won—use it!' This is a ball-availability cue, not a legal hands-in-the-ruck action.

frames.name: Win it and pass away
frames.notes: The winning side plays away. A2 passes the ball to A3, while A1 and D1 disengage and the others start returning to their lines. D1's shield changes to D3 as part of the rotation. In a match the ruck is over when the ball has been played out; the animation's ruck-marker membership can be tidied separately.

frames.name: Pass to coach and rotate
frames.notes: A3 passes to the coach to finish the repetition. D1 and D2 return, and D3 has the shield for the next turn. Check the pass goes to the intended target and players clear the working lane rather than crossing the path of the next pair.

frames.name: Reset for next repetition
frames.notes: Coach brings the ball back towards the starting spot and everyone resets. Swap jobs so players experience first support, shield resistance and playing the ball away. Ask one quick question before the next repetition: 'Who helped first, and who was ready to pass?'

drills.players: Eight players shown in two rotating groups of four, plus a coach. A1 is the first attacking support player; D1 holds the tackle shield and offers controlled resistance. A2 and D2 are the next players, ready for the outcome without joining the contact. Once attack secures the area, A2 plays the separate ball to A3, who passes to the coach. A4, D3 and D4 wait their turn and rotate through the jobs. Keep queues moving; use two stations if numbers or space allow.
drills.equipment: One sausage bag lying securely on the grass, one hand-held tackle shield for D1, one size 4 rugby ball positioned clear of the contact, four cones to mark the working area and a clear space for the receiving pass. The coach stands outside the running and contact lanes. Have a second ball ready for quick resets if available.
drills.instructions:
1. Explain the situation: 'Our player has been stopped. Don't watch—help us keep the ball.' Set A1 and D1 on opposite sides of the ground bag, with the shield held securely by D1. A2 and D2 are the next players; A3 is the receiver.
2. On the coach's cue, A1 and D1 approach under control. A1 establishes a balanced, on-feet contact position against the shield. Start with D1 offering very light, predictable resistance. A2 and D2 move to their waiting positions; neither joins the contact.
3. Allow a brief, controlled push–pull over the bag. For the demonstration, the attacking side wins: A1 holds the space and D1 gives ground. Do not let players charge, dive or try to throw each other off balance.
4. When you call 'Won—use it!', A2 plays the separate ball promptly and passes to A3. This ball is a safe training cue, not a ball being handled inside a live ruck.
5. A3 passes to the coach. Players leave the contact area, return to their lines and rotate the shield/contact/ball-playing roles. Repeat with a new first support player.
6. Before transferring this to a match-like game, reset the approach so support arrives from its own side of the breakdown; then introduce a realistic tackle and ball presentation only with appropriately coached, age-grade contact skills.
drills.coaching: Look for a reaction rather than a spectator: A1 goes as soon as a team-mate needs help; A2 gets into a useful position early. At contact, keep eyes up and the neck neutral, with head and shoulders above hips, a stable base, and short controlled leg steps. Bind with the arms—do not dive or launch the shoulder or head at the shield. A2 watches the ball, not the pushing, calls for it and passes accurately to A3 when released. The key question after each go is 'Did we get support there, and did we play away quickly?' A good rep is safe and tidy even if there is little movement over the bag.
drills.regression: Begin without opposition: A1 walks to the bag, stops in a strong position and calls 'Here'. Then put D1 behind the shield with no pushing and rehearse just the approach and posture. Add the loose ball and let A2 pass it to A3 on the coach's call. Reduce the queue and rotate often if children are waiting. Repeat slowly until heads stay up and everyone knows which side to enter from.
drills.progression: Move A1 a few metres farther away so they must react to a sudden 'tackle' call rather than start on a countdown. Increase D1's resistance a little only after technique is sound; keep the challenge about footwork and body shape, not collisions. Occasionally let the defending side win and ask D2 to play the separate ball while A2 reorganises—tell the players who won; do not assume the attackers always win. Finally try a small conditioned game starting from a safely coached tackle-and-presentation situation, with support arriving onside, legal age-grade ruck numbers and the next player using the ball quickly. Do not increase speed and force together.
drills.questions:
Who should react first when a team-mate is stopped?
Which side must you come from to join a real ruck?
Where should your eyes and head be when you meet the shield?
If A1 is protecting the ball, what is A2's job?
How do you know when the ball is available, and who can play it?
What changes if D1 wins instead of A1?
How is our ball placed beside the bag different from a ball inside a real ruck?
drills.notes: Coaching purpose: we lost possession because teammates were watching after tackles rather than supporting. Keep the message simple—'First there, on your feet, next player ready.' This animation is a rehearsed attacking win, not evidence that an opposed ruck will always be won. A1/D1 demonstrate the contact; A2 takes the ball placed to the side, A3 receives, and the coach collects it for the next repetition. D1's shield is passed to D3 during rotation. IMPORTANT before using the diagram to teach match laws: the A1 entry currently comes from the opposite side to the marked attack direction. Reposition the entry queues for a genuine onside support approach. Also review Step 4: A1 moves away after the contest while still listed as a member of the ruck marker; release the formation link once the ball is out when polishing the animation. The stated 8 minutes is practice time, not the sum of animation durations. These notes guide coaching but are not an RFU safety sign-off.

drills.title: Tackling rolling donut - basic
drills.objective: Track a moving tackle donut, get balanced before contact, and finish a controlled tackle. The aim is good feet and a safe wrap, not a big hit.
drills.safety: U10 supervised tackle practice. Use a properly padded donut and check the surface, space and equipment first. Start with slow, predictable rolls and only increase the challenge when each player can control their approach. Keep the waiting players and second coach outside the rolling/contact lane. Stop immediately for head-first contact, poor head position, loss of balance or an uncontrolled dive. Adults supervise and roll/reset the equipment; they are not the tackle target. No player-on-player contact or ruck follows this drill. Follow current RFU age-grade and club tackle guidance.

frames.name: Set up
frames.notes: Coach and donut at the release point. D1 leads the line; D2 and D3 wait behind the cones. The second coach watches from outside the lane. Check everyone is ready before starting.

frames.name: Chase
frames.notes: CHASE: D1 moves up towards the middle cone as the queue closes the gap behind. The donut stays still for now.

frames.name: Chill
frames.notes: CHILL: D1 settles into a low, balanced ready position with eyes on the donut. Short steps and control before the roll begins.

frames.name: Intercept rolling donut
frames.notes: KILL: the coach rolls the donut diagonally. D1 tracks it, adjusts the approach and makes a controlled shoulder-and-arms wrap, with the head safely to the side. Stop the roll without diving.

frames.name: Donut stopped
frames.notes: RESET: release the donut, regain balance and clear the contact area. Other players stay behind the cones.

frames.name: Return and rotate
frames.notes: RETURN: D1 loops back outside the working lane while the second coach helps get the donut back to its start. D2 becomes the next tackler once the lane is clear.

drills.players: 3 players in a queue (one working, two waiting); 2 coaches.
drills.equipment: 1 tackle donut, 3 cones, and a clear 10 × 8 m working area.
drills.instructions: Set up the players in a line behind the two back cones. The first player moves towards the middle cone on the CHASE call, then settles into a ready position on CHILL. Once the player is balanced and watching, the coach sends the donut on a slow, predictable diagonal roll. The player tracks it, adjusts their feet, makes a controlled tackle and stops the roll. On RESET, release the pad and get up. On RETURN, loop back outside the working lane while the coaches recover the donut; the next player moves to the front. One player goes at a time.
drills.coaching:
CHASE — eyes on the donut; close the distance without sprinting blindly.
CHILL — shorten the steps, keep the feet moving and get into a balanced, low position with eyes up.
KILL — meet the moving pad under control, keep the head safely to the side, make shoulder contact and wrap with the arms. Don't dive or lead with the head.
RESET — release, regain your feet and clear the lane.
Coach one thing at a time. If the approach is messy, slow the roll down.
drills.regression: Start with the donut stationary, or roll it very gently over a short distance. Bring the player closer and practise getting into position and wrapping before adding a moving target.
drills.progression: Vary which side the donut travels towards, or change the roll angle between turns. Have the tackler read the line and adjust their feet rather than guessing. Keep the roll slow enough for a safe tackle; only add speed when technique stays consistent.
drills.questions: When did you need to slow your feet? Where were you looking as the donut moved? Did you get close enough to wrap, or reach and dive? Where was your head at contact? Were you in control when you released?
drills.notes: The animation shows three players taking turns and two coaches, with one coach working the donut and the other observing/resetting from the side. CHASE–CHILL–KILL–RESET–RETURN are the on-pitch cues. The step timings are for the animation, not prescribed running speeds. Pause between turns for a quick correction; keep the other players behind the cones.
